name: Lemon juice whitening
lead: Lemon juice whitening is a home practice of applying lemon juice, alone or mixed with baking soda, to the teeth with the aim of removing surface stains and brightening their colour. It is shared as a natural, inexpensive alternative to peroxide whitening products, and people who use it do so to get a lighter, cleaner-looking smile.

Lemon juice is about 5 to 6 percent citric acid, with more than lime and several times more than orange juice.[1] Dental sources associate acidic foods and drinks, including citrus, with dental erosion.[2] No clinical trials of lemon juice as a tooth whitener were found. Human whitening trials have tested peroxide products.[4]

paras: Proponents say the acid and the fruit's reputation as a natural bleach lighten tooth colour. Lemon juice is described in general sources as being used to lighten hair in sunlight [1], and some extend the idea to teeth. The encyclopedic lemon article does not mention teeth [1].

Professional and over-the-counter whitening mostly relies on hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide, with in-office treatments reported to improve tooth shade by two to seven shades and home strips by one or two shades over about two weeks.[4] Whitening toothpastes use abrasives and detergents rather than bleach.[4] Wikipedia's tooth whitening article describes baking soda as a low-abrasive stain remover that showed no adverse effects in clinical studies, and it does not list lemon among home remedies.[4]

Acid has a long history in tooth care folklore. The same article notes that in the late 1600s barbers filed teeth and applied acid, which it says eroded teeth and increased decay, and that other historical remedies included honey, burnt salt with vinegar, and oxalic acid proposed in 1877.[4] Historical references to lemon on teeth specifically are not documented.

Dental erosion is the irreversible loss of tooth structure through chemical dissolution by acids not of bacterial origin. It starts in the enamel and can progress to dentin, which gives teeth a duller yellow look and can cause sensitivity.[2] Foods and drinks with a pH below about 5.0 to 5.7 can trigger erosion, and fruit juices resist the buffering effect of saliva more than many drinks, so they may prolong the drop in mouth pH.[2]

The article reports that how often acidic food or drink is consumed matters more than total volume, that swishing acidic liquids in the mouth increases the risk of widespread erosion, and that sucking citrus fruit can contribute.[2] It lists citric acid in orange juice among extrinsic sources and does not name lemon juice specifically.[2] Dental erosion often occurs together with abrasion from vigorous brushing.[2]
No studies found. Whitening trials in humans have tested peroxide products [4].

Dental erosion is irreversible loss of tooth structure by non-bacterial acids. Citrus fruit and fruit juices are discussed among dietary causes, with frequency of exposure and swishing acidic liquids increasing risk [2]. When enamel is lost and dentin is exposed, dentin hypersensitivity can result, and dental guidance includes limiting acidic foods and waiting before brushing [3].

Lemon juice and baking soda is a recurring item in natural whitening roundups and home-remedy lists. Proponents describe it as cheap and available in any kitchen. Dental sources describe acid contact with enamel as the mechanism of erosion,[2] and guidance on dentin sensitivity includes limiting acidic foods and waiting before brushing.[3] Wikipedia also describes an unhealthy preoccupation with whitening, sometimes called bleachorexia, which it compares to body dysmorphic disorder.[4]

card.summary: Lemon juice on teeth is a popular natural whitening idea; no trials were found and citric acid is a known erosion factor.
card.note: Citric acid is associated with enamel erosion.

quick.overview:
Lemon juice whitening means putting lemon juice, sometimes with baking soda, on the teeth to remove stains.
No clinical trials were found. Lemon juice is highly acidic, and dental sources link acidic foods and juices to enamel erosion.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say citric acid bleaches or dissolves stains. No research tests this; acids are also the mechanism of dental erosion.
quick.risks: Erosion is irreversible and may expose dentin, causing sensitivity. Dental sources note exposure frequency matters.

chain: Lemon juice applied to teeth, sometimes with baking soda
Acid and mild abrasion said to lift surface stain
angle.text: Users rub or rinse lemon juice, often followed or mixed with baking soda, on the teeth in the belief that the acid lifts stain and bleaches them. The aim is a whiter smile without buying whitening products.
